headline: Nvidia's leadership upheaval and a roughly $4.2tn rout in AI infrastructure stocks set the tone before Nvidia's first earnings without Jensen Huang and the Anthropic IPO. Rate-hike talk in the US and UK and a credit market that is getting choosier add to the strain.
watch: Nvidia's first earnings since Jensen Huang's resignation, and any guidance on China exposure and export rules
Anthropic IPO pricing and demand, with activists and some retail investors openly uneasy
The Shenzhen Apec summit, where Trump and US tech executives are expected to meet, and any export-control signals
Fed and Bank of England rate commentary after the hints at a larger December Fed hike and the BoE's move to 4%
Fallout from Friday's FAA ground stop and any accountability for contractor L3Harris

paragraphs.text: Biotech capital markets sent mixed signals. Fierce Biotech reports that Sanofi-backed Windward Bio priced its IPO at exactly its $225 million target to fund two respiratory drugs licensed from China, and TradingView confirms it is now listed on Nasdaq. Fierce adds that Rezera put off its own listing, citing market conditions, and Axios also lists Rezera bailing on its IPO. The same Axios roundup mentions a $1.5 billion Pfizer item and a Delix funding, but the headline gives no detail, so the nature of the Pfizer deal is unclear. The WSJ also reports a $1.15 billion M&A deal for preclinical company Unnatural Products, with no terms available here. The window is open for names with a clear story and partner backing, but it is not open to everyone.

paragraphs.text: Smaller transactions and restructurings continued. Charles River is paying $470 million upfront for two Frontage bioanalysis labs in Pennsylvania from Tigermed, per Fierce Biotech. Cellectis will cut 70% of its workforce as it moves from allogeneic CAR-Ts to in vivo therapies. Bristol Myers Squibb's research chief is leaving amid an R&D reorganization, and Summit Therapeutics let go several launch team members, including its commercial chief, ahead of what Fierce calls a high-stakes FDA decision. AstraZeneca has cut about 600 US respiratory and immunology sales jobs under its $1.5 billion savings plan, per Bloomberg via Fierce Pharma. On the clinical side, Rezolute's phase 3 in tumor hyperinsulinism hit its primary endpoint ahead of an FDA meeting on another indication, and AstraZeneca widened Imfinzi into cisplatin-ineligible bladder cancer with a Padcev combination, keeping pressure on Keytruda.

paragraphs.text: Elsewhere in pharma, Teva held its first R&D day, and one analyst team came away more confident even while conceding the peak-sales estimates for late-stage assets look aspirational. Bavarian Nordic's CFO is stepping down just as a new CEO arrives, despite a Q3 beat. Fierce also launched a weekly oral GLP-1 tracker, with Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill both seeing rising prescriptions. Europe's CHMP backed AstraZeneca's Baxfendy and gave Hansoh's Aumseqa a second chance. Separately, Fierce Pharma Asia flags concern that a draft US Treasury policy restricting some US investment in China is too ambiguous and could backfire, which matters for anyone doing China licensing deals.

paragraphs.text: Policy and providers had a harder week. The administration is giving states an optional grace period on Medicaid work requirements until June 30, 2027, instead of enforcing them from January 1, per the NYT and Fierce Healthcare. The WSJ reports the White House ordered officials this summer to release millions of dollars of detained Chinese vapes after talks involving Trump adviser Chris LaCivita and his son, who are helping the Geek Bar importer. The WSJ also reports the Pan American Health Organization has revoked the US measles elimination status, according to people familiar. CommonSpirit posted a $544 million operating loss to open fiscal 2027, blaming a weaker payer mix and rising costs despite good volumes. Ardent Health is buying Missouri nonprofit Boone Health for $47 million, with a $200 million, 10-year capital commitment and at least $30 million of annual EBITDA expected by year three. The CCI has cleared an Advent-backed stake purchase in Yatharth Hospitals. Fierce also notes that new federal caps on student borrowing are starting to shape medical school plans.

The NYT also covers brain implants that let ALS patients speak and sing.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia dominates. Huang's resignation, which the NYT says shocked Taiwan, follows reports of an alleged affair with a Chinese spy, according to the FT. The FT says the episode has increased momentum in Congress for tighter AI chip export rules. The NYT and CNBC raise conflict questions around Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose family business has ties to Nvidia and to Southeast Asian data-center clients now affected by chip rules he is writing. The FT's Alphaville questions the independence of Nvidia's board. The FT also says the company has made itself a long list of adversaries. Yahoo Finance flags Nvidia's first earnings in the post-Huang era as the key event of the week, alongside the Anthropic IPO, and la Repubblica calls the pair a crucial test of the market's AI bet. Details on guidance are not yet available.

paragraphs.text: The AI trade is already wobbling. The FT says data-center construction stocks have lost $4.2tn in value as the tech sell-off hits picks-and-shovels names, and its chart of the week describes a rotation into defensive sectors. CNBC ETF strategists suggest the Nvidia turmoil and a Democratic Congress could shift AI demand toward other big tech names and rival chipmakers. In South Korea, Chosunbiz and BigGo report that a slump in the KOSPI and chip stocks is raising principal-loss risk on high-yield equity-linked notes sold near the 9000 level, which come due next month. Bloomberg reports State Street and Pictet are calling an end to Europe's outperformance, which had been helped by AI-related stumbles elsewhere. The FT suggests Chinese tech could offer AI exposure with less drama. Berkshire Hathaway hit a record high with a 19% fourth-quarter rally, CNBC says, and CNBC notes Canadian stocks are up more than 1% since the midterms while the S&P 500 is down 0.5%.

paragraphs.text: Rates are the other pressure point. The FT says Fed policymakers have floated a larger hike in December after strong jobs, growth and inflation data. Bank of England chief economist Huw Pill told the FT that last week's quarter-point rise to 4% was significant but that there is further to go. The FT also says the low-hire, low-fire labor market is weighing on US and UK productivity. The WSJ warns of another wave of food inflation from energy costs and supply-chain delays, and writes about the one in five US mortgage holders locked into 3% rates. Bloomberg describes crypto's slow selloff pushing bitcoin toward its yearly lows as major demand sources weaken.

paragraphs.text: Politics and geopolitics frame the week. Following Democratic midterm wins, the FT says the party is shifting toward economic themes, and Bloomberg and MarketWatch point to possible changes on Social Security and Medicare. NYT DealBook and the FT preview next week's Shenzhen summit with Trump and US tech executives, where trade, export controls and suspected spying are on the agenda. Friday's FAA ground stop, which the WSJ attributes to a data overload on an aging router network in Arkansas and the FT calls the result of long neglect, caused a third day of cancellations. The WSJ says the work was routine copper-wire replacement, and authorities are focused on contractor L3Harris. On luxury, the WSJ reports Gucci is cutting prices while Louis Vuitton resists. SpaceX caught a Starship after its return from orbit, a milestone toward full reusability.

paragraphs.text: Investment-grade and high-yield investors are looking for shelter. Bloomberg's Credit Weekly says US corporate bonds have been rallying in recent weeks as money managers seek refuge from stock-market turbulence, with yields around 6% drawing interest after the Nvidia drama. Yahoo Finance, though, describes credit tightening in a note about KKR and Blue Owl shares, which suggests alternative asset managers are being watched for signs of stress. We have only the headline for that piece. Jamie Dimon's five-stage warning on whether an AI bubble could become a credit crisis is circulating, again with little detail in the list. Several seasonal-return pages for high-yield funds are in the feed, but they carry no news.

paragraphs.text: Private credit is the quiet theme. The AFR argues its illiquidity cannot be engineered away, a pointed view as the asset class reaches more retail and semi-liquid vehicles. In South Korea, Bloomberg-style coverage via Bloomingbit says the financial regulator wants to limit private credit loans to active-duty soldiers to curb crypto-fueled debt. Tokenized private credit led sector gains in crypto markets, per TokenPost, and a Form 4 shows a 10% owner activity in Audax Private Credit Fund, with no detail beyond the filing. Apollo declared its quarterly dividend, which is routine but a sign of payout stability.

paragraphs.text: Individual borrower stress is visible at the margins. The FT says Trump Media faces a $1 billion debt crunch as its bitcoin bet fades, and the plunge in its shares and crypto prices could force asset sales or costly new debt. CNBC reports Foundation Future Industries, an Eric Trump-backed robot startup, missed payroll after the founder borrowed $4.6 million from the company to buy a home. The FT says hedge fund stumbles show the dangers of hot money, where growth was pursued without enough risk management. Separately, the FT says the head of the European Banking Authority is moving away from a single deposit insurance scheme and working on other ways to free up cross-border lending.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO is the dominant deal story, and coverage so far is about sentiment rather than terms. The NYT calls the prospectus unusually candid about existential risk, and its opinion video argues there is a flaw at the heart of the offering. The WSJ says some individual investors are cool on AI but find it hard to sit out a trillion-dollar listing, with one calling it the last chopper out of Saigon. Business Insider reports activists are protesting the offering, with one comparing it to a game of Jenga. For bankers, demand will be tested against a backdrop of falling AI infrastructure stocks and Nvidia's coming results. Pricing, size and timing are not given in what we have.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia-backed Firmus Grid is planning a $3 billion private fundraising after pulling its IPO, per Traders Union and Investing.com UK. That shows how quickly the AI infrastructure IPO window narrowed. Taken with the Rezera delay in biotech and Windward's on-target pricing, it suggests investors are picking carefully rather than shutting issuers out.

paragraphs.text: Private capital is active in the Gulf despite a lull. The FT reports Brookfield and KKR are in advanced talks and competing over a roughly $700 million majority stake in eyewear chain Eyewa, ending what it calls a Middle East deal drought. Closer to home, Car Dealership Guy News says dealership buyers are paying up for the right brands and strong numbers. The FT also says HSBC is experimenting with bots in wealth management, which could shift competition among wealth firms. The FT's piece on Samsung's move from AI chips into data centers points to the same infrastructure theme that is now under market pressure.
